title: What a Gursikh does
hook: Bhai Gurdas pictures the Sikh who rises early, bathes, remembers, joins the sangat and works honestly

segments.voice: Yesterday, a roll of honor, and your line, ordinary names remembered. Whose name did you say out loud? Day seven hundred nine.

What would a stranger learn about you from watching one ordinary day? Not your opinions. Just the day: what time the light went on, what you did first, where you went, how you earned your bread. Yesterday Bhai Gurdas gave us names. Today he gives us the shape of a day, the day of a Sikh who belongs to the Guru. And he doesn't describe it with a list of beliefs. He describes it with a clock. Today's word: Gursikh.
screen: `ONE ORDINARY DAY, WATCHED.` → `NOT OPINIONS, JUST THE DAY.` → `A DAY TOLD BY THE CLOCK.`

segments.voice: Gursikh puts two words together: Gur, the Guru, and Sikh. A Sikh of the Guru. Bhai Gurdas returns to this person in his vars, and the picture he paints is practical, almost a timetable. The Gursikh rises while the night is still on, in the early hours. Bathes. Then remembers: sits with the Guru's word, with the Name, before the day's noise starts. Then goes to the sangat, the gathering, to sit with others and hear and sing the Guru's hymns. And then goes to work, and earns a living honestly, and shares what comes in. That's it. No mountain top, no cave. A house, a gathering, a workplace. The picture has deep roots in the Guru's own word. In the Guru Granth Sahib, on Ang three hundred five, Guru Ram Das describes the one who calls himself a Sikh of the Guru: rising early, bathing, meditating on the Name, and then carrying the Guru's word through the rest of the day. Bhai Gurdas, in his vars, fills in the day around that morning. Turn it over, and three things stand out. First, the order. Remembering comes before the work, so the work happens inside the remembering, not instead of it. Second, the company. The Gursikh's day isn't solitary: the sangat is part of the schedule, not an extra. And third, the money. Honest work is in the picture on purpose. In Bhai Gurdas's picture, holiness doesn't leave the marketplace. It walks into it with clean hands. A Gursikh, in this telling, isn't known by a title. You'd know one by watching the day.
screen: `GUR AND SIKH: A SIKH OF THE GURU.` · `RISE, BATHE, REMEMBER.` · `THE SANGAT, THEN HONEST WORK.` · `KNOWN BY THE SHAPE OF A DAY.` · then, large: `THE GURSIKH'S DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rise a little earlier. Not tonight's resolution, tomorrow's small change. Use the sit to plan it. Pick a time, ten or fifteen minutes before your usual alarm. Picture the house when it's still quiet. Picture what you'll do with those minutes before the phone: wash your face, sit, breathe, read a line that matters to you. Keep it small enough that you'll actually do it. If you pray, you can choose a line of the Guru's word or say Waheguru in that quiet. The bell holds the time.
Gursikh. A Sikh of the Guru. In Bhai Gurdas's vars, someone you'd recognize by the day: rising early, remembering, sitting in the sangat, working honestly.
Your line: the gursikh's day. Tonight, set the alarm a little earlier, and tomorrow, give the first quiet minutes to remembering. Day seven hundred nine.

howItsDone: Sikh custom keeps the amrit vela, the hours before dawn, for bathing and reciting or listening to the morning banis before the day's work.

fork.setup: you want to live as a Sikh of the Guru. where does your day start?
options: at work, as early as possible.
rising early, bathing, and remembering the Name.
late, after a long night of reading.
fork.reveal: Guru Ram Das (Ang 305) starts the Sikh's day early: rising, bathing, remembering the Name. Bhai Gurdas adds the sangat and honest work around it.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: a Sikh of the Guru, from gur and sikh.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Gursikh is a very strict Sikh.
what it means: a Sikh of the Guru, recognized by the shape of a day: rising, remembering, sangat, honest work.
what a scholar hears: Bhai Gurdas fills out a morning already in the Guru Granth Sahib, where Guru Ram Das describes the Sikh who rises early, on Ang 305.

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas (the Gursikh's day, e.g. Var 40, pauri 11)

notes: Bhai Gurdas pauri reference uncertain: the Gursikh who rises in the last watch of the night, bathes, recites/remembers, goes to the sangat and earns honestly appears in several vars (e.g. Var 40 pauri 11; Var 12). Please confirm the best single citation.
Ang 305–306 paraphrased: Guru Ram Das, 'gur satgur ka jo sikh akhae...' (rises early, bathes in the pool of nectar, meditates on the Name, sings the Guru's word through the day). Confirm the Ang.
'Gursikh puts two words together: Gur and Sikh' is a compound, not an etymological claim; confirm phrasing.
howItsDone describes the amrit vela as Sikh custom; confirm phrasing.
Editor pass: cut the gloss 'Sikh, the learner' (word-origin claim) and the sweeping 'again and again'; softened 'takes that morning and fills in the whole day' to a plainer statement.
